Cet1 contains a topologically closed β-barrel with 8 parallel β-strands that form an interior tunnel with a diameter of approximately 6Å, and that the tunnel is the catalytic active site of the enzyme.

the triphosphate hydrolysis reaction is a highly concerted event that involves the concerted action of 15 side chains in the triphosphate-tunnel active site.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the active site is composed of a complex network of interactions between the substrate, the metal ion, and the side chains of the protein.
the active site of Cet1 is composed of 15 residues, each with a specific function, and that the 8-strand tunnel is a highly efficient conduit for substrate delivery to the γ phosphate.

the catalytic mechanism of Cet1 involves a metal-dependent hydrolysis reaction in which the metal is coordinated by the γ phosphate and by a triad of active site residues (Asp377, Lys409, and Asp471), and a water molecule is activated by a network of 7 side chains (Asp377 and Arg458, Glu433 and Arg469, Arg393, Thr473, and Lys409) for nucleophilic attack on the γ phosphate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the active site of RNA triphosphates is more elaborate than the canonical metalloenzyme active sites that have been studied to date.
the catalytic mechanism of RNA triphosphates is highly complex and requires a large number of active site residues.
the active site of yeast RNA triphosphates is highly specialized and optimized to catalyze γ phosphate hydrolyses in the context of a topologically complex, hydrophilic, and relatively rigid tunnel.
